title: The Miners Who Invented Chilean Democracy
event_summary: On December 21, 1907, thousands of nitrate miners—mostly indigenous Aymara, Bolivian, and Peruvian workers—marched into the port city of Iquique to demand fair wages and safer working conditions in the brutal saltpeter mines of the Atacama Desert. They gathered peacefully in the Santa María School courtyard with their families. Chilean General Roberto Silva Renard ordered troops to open fire with machine guns, killing an estimated 2,000 to 3,600 men, women, and children in what became known as the Santa María School Massacre.
why_forgotten: The Chilean government actively suppressed accounts of the massacre for decades, destroying official records and intimidating witnesses. The nitrate industry was dominated by British capital, and both British and Chilean elites had financial incentives to minimize the event. It was largely erased from national textbooks until the late 20th century, and the multi-ethnic, working-class identity of the victims made them easy to overlook in elite-driven historiography.
why_it_matters: The massacre radicalized an entire generation of Chilean workers and directly catalyzed the formation of Latin America's most powerful labor movements and socialist parties, ultimately leading to Salvador Allende's election in 1970—the first democratically elected Marxist head of state. The event established the template for labor-versus-capital conflicts across the Global South and remains a touchstone for modern debates about multinational corporate responsibility in developing nations. Chile's current constitution-rewriting process still echoes demands first articulated by those miners.
